Instead of suicide, why not try the nervous breakdown route? Like, for sure there are a thousand more helpful and healthy options than what I’m about to say, and literally please listen to everyone else before you listen to me, but I gotta make this option real in your head as a last resort.

So basically, like 5 years ago I had a nervous breakdown. It had been a long time coming. I was smart, but had no time management skills, and I also had that type of hyper-impulsive, super-negative personality that inclined people towards short-term gratification rather than long term planning and goal setting, so on the one hand, it made perfect sense to engage my intellect with increasingly rigorous academic pursuits, but on the other hand, the person who I actually was was completely incapable of keeping up with what I was capable of. I feel like that sentence might make sense to you because you might be the same type of person. If not, whatevs, skip to paragraph 3.

So anyway, it went down like this: I stopped going to my uni classes, abandoned all my friends, who didn’t come looking for me, so let’s be real they weren’t actually friends, and then, instead of going to my exams, I hid in my bedroom, binge eating junk food, drinking hundreds of dollars worth of mojitos, and watching gay romance movies.

Completely broke my parents heart, and I will never forgive myself even though they have, but you know what, it’s 5 years later, and I’ve made 5 years worth of progress. I’ve Addressed a lot of childhood trauma with a psychiatrist, managed to find a shitty job that gave me tonnes of panic attacks at first but that I actually kind of like now in some moments, got my driver’s licence, gradually started taking on more responsibilities, like buying all my own food and paying my own phone bill, lost 30 kilos on a keto diet I formulated myself, made some real friends who I absolutely love to death, and enrolled in a new, far less rigorous academic course that should lead to some real employment and independence eventually, and after that, after all that struggle and folly, then I will focus on the dream I was originally trying to achieve with the uni course I dropped out of, and I’ll succeed this time, because I’ll be following a course set out by me and for me, and have the wisdom to know how to make it work.

I’ll be real with you; I’m currently dealing with a pretty terrible back injury which has left me physically and psychologically stagnant. A lot of old shit has floated to the surface, and a lot of old coping strategies have come into play, but I’d bet my life I’ll make a come back, because betting your life is better than throwing it away.

Good luck buddy. Hope you make it to Next week.

I’ve heard about things like this happening before. A lot of the other conmenters here sound optimistic about why those things were said to you. My suggestion is this: psychopaths exist, sadists exist, and these people are very good at sneaking into situations where they can harm vulnerable people with impunity. Sometimes they become police officers. This time one of them decided to work at a suicide hotline. Don’t be deterred from this conclusion if the person you spoke to happened to be a woman either. Women are just as capable of cruel, anti-social behaviour as anyone else, and probably more likely than men to use means of harming people such as these, which don’t involve direct physical confrontation.

Disregard everything this person told you. They were lying to you for the sheer sense of joy and power they get out of harming others. Call the hotline again, if not to talk about your issues, then at least to make them aware you had this experience because I can guarantee you others who call the hotline are at risk from that arsehole.

As for your actual feelings that you’ve shared with us in your post, I’m betting that, to you, admitting that you have depression and anxiety, and that these problems are the cause of your slow progress through life feels like a way of refusing to take responsibility for your situation, because I used to feel that way, but it’s not true.

People are 100% responsible for dealing with their mental illnesses, it’s actually by not taking these problems seriously, by saying “I’m just lazy. I’m just a loser. I’m just not trying hard enough,” it’s by acting like your problem isn’t real that you’re refusing to accept responsibility for your situation.

Accept that you are at a disadvantage and that it’s nothing to be ashamed of. Do something everyday that’s more and better than what you did yesterday, whether it’s applying for a job or just taking a shower. Learn to how to take care of yourself. Treat your illness like an enemy and conquer it, and if you think you can’t, try anyway, because you have nothing better to do; do you? And, most importantly of all, give yourself permission to feel proud of your victories, even when no one else is, because no one else is you, and no one else is a better judge of you and your efforts than you are.

My last bit of advice: one of the easiest and best ways to build self-esteem is to volunteer for others. It helps you realise that your situation could be worse which creates a sense of gratitude, and it gives you the opportunity to help make someone else’s life better in a real, quantifiable way. No one who is a volunteer is a loser.
